paper.title: Virtual Node Graph Neural Network for Full Phonon Prediction
paper.research_summary: The paper introduces the Virtual Node Graph Neural Network (VGNN) to predict phonon spectra and bandstructures directly from atomic coordinates, addressing challenges of variable-length output and complex unit cells. It presents three variants—vector (VVN), matrix (MVN), and momentum-dependent matrix (k-MVN) virtual nodes—to predict Γ-point phonons and full phonon dispersion. The models are trained on ab initio DFPT phonon data and validated on diverse alloy systems; MVN is used to build a Γ-phonon database of 146,000+ Materials Project materials.

tasks.objective: Predict phonon spectra and full phonon band structures directly from atomic coordinates
constraints: no prior knowledge of interatomic forces
output_goal: 3m Γ-phonon energies for m atoms per unit cell
full phonon band structure at arbitrary k points in the Brillouin zone

evidence.text: By developing three types of virtual node approaches - the vector, matrix, and momentum-dependent matrix virtual nodes, we achieve direct prediction of Γ-phonon spectra and full dispersion only using atomic coordinates as input.
We study materials’ phonon spectra and dispersion relations, given that phonons bands are challenging to compute or measure with high computational cost and limited experimental resources.

Here we present the virtual node graph neural network to address the challenges. By developing three types of virtual node approaches - the vector, matrix, and momentum-dependent matrix virtual nodes, we achieve direct prediction of Γ-phonon spectra and full dispersion only using atomic coordinates as input.

stages.stage_name_raw: Phonon data acquisition from ab initio databases
stages.stage_goal: Acquire high-quality phonon data for training and validation
stage_output: phonon dispersion along highly symmetric paths

evidence.text: We trained all of our models against an ab initio DFPT computational database for phonon dispersion in harmonic model25. The data set contains material structures (the same as the primitive structure obtained from the Material Project12), second-order derivatives of energies with respect to atomic perturbations for regular points inside the irreducible zone, and phonon dispersion along highly symmetric paths of 1,521 crystalline inorganic materials.
We also got phonon dispersion of complex (more number of atoms per unit cell) materials from Atsushi Togo’s phonon database31.

stages.stage_goal: Prepare, filter, and split phonon datasets for training, validation, and testing
stage_output: complex-material test set (156 materials with >40 atoms/unit cell)

evidence.text: The data set contains material structures (the same as the primitive structure obtained from the Material Project12), second-order derivatives of energies with respect to atomic perturbations for regular points inside the irreducible zone, and phonon dispersion along highly symmetric paths of 1,521 crystalline inorganic materials. These materials have 2 to 40 atoms per unit cell, with an average of 7.38. For this work, we only used the highly symmetric path phonon dispersion as our training data. The dispersion is between wave vectors⃗k in the fractional reciprocal unit and response spectra in cm−1. All models randomly split the data into 90% training (1,365 materials), and 10% testing (156 materials) sets.

We also got phonon dispersion of complex (more number of atoms per unit cell) materials from Atsushi Togo’s phonon database31. ... We selected materials whose lowest Γ-phonon band is higher than −0.07 cm−1. We also filtered the material to get only the ones with more than 40 atoms per unit cell. Finally, we randomly selected 156 (the same as the number of data in the testing set for ease of comparison) out of 505 filtered materials.

stages.stage_goal: Optimize neural network parameters to minimize prediction error on phonon data

evidence.text: The model is optimized by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) loss function between the phonon of the training data set and the one predicted by the model after normalizing them by the maximum phonon frequency of each material.
We optimize the values of the training parameters. The set of parameters that gives the best results for VVN, MVN, k-MVN are shown in Table S1.
